items.title: Application by Matthew Milat (s 78 review) [2026] NSWSC 966 — a child offender's 43-year sentence not referred
items.citation: [2026] NSWSC 966 (Dhanji J, on the papers, 12 August 2026)
items.significance: Sentenced at about 17 years 11 months to 43 years for murder, Matthew Milat sought an inquiry into his sentence after his appeals ended; none of his complaints raised a doubt, so the application was refused.
items.document: Cases/Crime/Application by Matthew Milat (s 78 review) [2026] NSWSC 966 - Case Summary.pdf
items.document11: Cases/Year 11/Year 11 - Application by Matthew Milat (s 78 review) [2026] NSWSC 966 - Case Summary.pdf
items.lead:
**Matthew Milat** was about **17 years 11 months** old at the time of the 2010 offence; his co-offender was 18. He pleaded
guilty in the Children's Court and was sentenced in 2012 to **43 years** (non-parole **30**). The CCA dismissed his appeal
in 2014 (and reduced the co-offender's sentence); the High Court refused special leave. In 2026, self-represented, he applied
under **s 78** for an inquiry or a referral to the CCA.
items.use_it_for:
- **crime.5.4** — sentencing a child offender as an adult for the most serious crime; CROC's "shortest appropriate time".
- **crime.4.8 / crime.4.5** — the review mechanism after appeals are exhausted.
items.caution: A **class case summary**. The killing is not described; no birth date is in the file.

sections.Held — refused on the papers:
- An order needs a **doubt or question** about guilt, mitigating circumstances or evidence (**s 79(2)**); the test is unease or
  disquiet. **Section 78 is not another appeal.**
- His complaints — parity with the co-offender, the plea discount, drugs, risk, his surname, premeditation, and being
  "treated as an adult" though a child — had largely been dealt with before and raised no such doubt.
sections.Use it for:
- **crime.5.4** — sentencing a child offender as an adult for the most serious crime; CROC's "shortest appropriate time".
- **crime.4.8 / crime.4.5** — the review mechanism after appeals are exhausted.
sections.Caution: A **class case summary**. The killing is not described; no birth date is in the file.

items.title: Brooker v R [2026] NSWCCA 181 — one phrase, two readings, and no inferred error
items.citation: [2026] NSWCCA 181 (Dhanji J, Ward ACJ and Yehia J agreeing; 6 November 2026)
items.significance: A drug supplier argued the judge used other offending to inflate the seriousness of his offence; the Court would not infer error from words open to two readings.
items.document: Cases/Crime/Brooker v R [2026] NSWCCA 181 - Case Summary.pdf
items.document11: Cases/Year 11/Year 11 - Brooker v R [2026] NSWCCA 181 - Case Summary.pdf
items.lead:
**Brodie Brooker** pleaded guilty to **ongoing supply** (19 supplies, May 2024), possessing a stun gun and attempting to
receive **280 g** of methylamphetamine, with **11 offences on Form 1s**. In December 2025 he received an aggregate **4
years 3 months** (non-parole 2 years 7 months).
items.use_it_for:
- **crime.4.3** — objective seriousness and the use of Form 1 (taken-into-account) offences.
- **crime.4.5** — how appeal courts read sentencing remarks.
items.caution: A **class case summary**; only Dhanji J gave reasons.

sections.Held — leave granted, appeal dismissed:
- He argued that calling the attempt "**not an isolated aberration**" wrongly used other offending to raise **objective
  seriousness**. The phrase has two readings; an appeal court will **not infer error** where the remarks are reasonably
  read as lawful.
- Calling the quantity "just into the commercial range" but "still a very large amount" was not an error either.
sections.Use it for:
- **crime.4.3** — objective seriousness and the use of Form 1 (taken-into-account) offences.
- **crime.4.5** — how appeal courts read sentencing remarks.
sections.Caution: A **class case summary**; only Dhanji J gave reasons.

items.title: Gatt v R [2026] NSWCCA 182 — unchallenged expert evidence rejected without warning
items.citation: [2026] NSWCCA 182 (Roberts J, with N Adams CJ at CL; Dhanji J agreeing on error; 6 November 2026)
items.significance: An aggregate sentence for 20 domestic violence and public justice offences fell from 12 to 11 years because the judge rejected an expert's unchallenged evidence without warning — a practical injustice.
items.document: Cases/Crime/Gatt v R [2026] NSWCCA 182 - Case Summary.pdf
items.document11: Cases/Year 11/Year 11 - Gatt v R [2026] NSWCCA 182 - Case Summary.pdf
items.lead:
**Adrian Gatt** pleaded guilty to **20** domestic violence and public justice offences, including a day of assaults on his
wife and children (31 May 2023) and, from custody, having family press his wife to withdraw her statement. In September
2024 he received an aggregate **12 years** (non-parole 8).
items.use_it_for:
- **crime.4.5 (appeals)** — error, resentencing and a split court on the number.
- **Procedural fairness** — a judge must give a party a chance to answer before rejecting uncontested evidence.
items.caution: A **class case summary**; family violence offending against a wife and children. The judges split on the final sentence.

sections.Held — appeal allowed (one of four groun:
- Grounds 1–2 failed: the finding that a "perverted" patriarchal motive raised his moral culpability was open.
- **Ground 3 upheld:** the judge rejected **unchallenged expert evidence** of harsh childhood discipline **without warning**
  the defence — a **practical injustice** (procedural fairness).
- Ground 4 (weight given to his minor record) failed.
- **Resentenced: 11 years, non-parole 7.** Dhanji J would have set 10 years (non-parole 6 years 6 months).
sections.Use it for:
- **crime.4.5 (appeals)** — error, resentencing and a split court on the number.
- **Procedural fairness** — a judge must give a party a chance to answer before rejecting uncontested evidence.
sections.Caution: A **class case summary**; family violence offending against a wife and children. The judges split on the final sentence.

items.title: R v Xerri (a pseudonym) [2026] NSWCCA 183 — are emails 'property' for self-defence?
items.citation: [2026] NSWCCA 183 (Muston J, with N Adams CJ at CL and Cavanagh J; 6 November 2026)
items.significance: A man acquitted on appeal by arguing he grabbed a device to protect his emails lost that acquittal: on the facts found, emails were information, not property, and reading them aloud was not interference.
items.document: Cases/Crime/R v Xerri (a pseudonym) [2026] NSWCCA 183 - Case Summary.pdf
items.document11: Cases/Year 11/Year 11 - R v Xerri (a pseudonym) [2026] NSWCCA 183 - Case Summary.pdf
items.lead:
After a separation, the respondent's emails were read aloud from a family device (20 November 2023); he took the
device and grabbed an arm. He was convicted in the Local Court of **common assault** and contravening an **ADVO**. On
appeal the District Court held the emails were **property**, so he could rely on **self-defence of property**
(s 418(2)(c)), and acquitted him. The DPP had four questions stated to the CCA.
items.use_it_for:
- **crime.3.8 (defences)** — the limits of self-defence of property; statutory definitions doing the work.
- **Year 11 (Changing the law)** — courts adapting old property concepts to technology (judicial methods).
items.caution: A **class case summary** of a narrow ruling on stated facts; guilt is not decided. Pseudonyms; domestic violence context.

sections.Held:
- On the **limited facts** found, the emails were **information, not property**: property is definable, identifiable by
  others and has some permanence (*Ainsworth*); mere information is not (contrast Bitcoin, *Yeates* (Vic 2025), and online
  game tokens, *Lakeman* (UK 2026)).
- Reading them aloud was not **interference** with property.
- The acquittal was **quashed** and the appeal **remitted** to the District Court; the other two questions were not answered.
  The Court stressed the ruling is confined to the facts stated.
sections.Use it for:
- **crime.3.8 (defences)** — the limits of self-defence of property; statutory definitions doing the work.
- **Year 11 (Changing the law)** — courts adapting old property concepts to technology (judicial methods).
sections.Caution: A **class case summary** of a narrow ruling on stated facts; guilt is not decided. Pseudonyms; domestic violence context.

items.title: State of NSW v Mustapha [2026] NSWSC 1406 — a third terrorism supervision order sought
items.significance: Despite compliance and progress, a man never convicted of a terrorism offence was found to pose a continuing unacceptable risk, so the court made a 28-day interim supervision order pending examinations.
items.document: Cases/Crime/State of NSW v Mustapha [2026] NSWSC 1406 - Case Summary.pdf
items.document11: Cases/Year 11/Year 11 - State of NSW v Mustapha [2026] NSWSC 1406 - Case Summary.pdf
items.lead:
**Mejid Mustapha**, 37, has a violent record and past extremist beliefs (in 2018 he assaulted a police officer and made
threats referring to Islamic State) but has **never been convicted of a terrorism offence**. He was placed on an extended
supervision order in 2022 and a second, relaxed one-year order in November 2025. The State sought a **third**.
items.use_it_for:
- **crime.4.8** — NSW's high-risk terrorism offender scheme; supervision of people not convicted of terrorism.
- **Balance** — liberty and rehabilitation against community protection.
items.caution: A **class case summary of an interim order**; the allegations and any final order are undecided.

sections.Held — Schmidt AJ:
- The test is an unacceptable risk of a **serious terrorism offence**, not violence in general.
- Despite his compliance and progress, lingering beliefs and recent conduct meant, if the allegations were proved, a further
  order could be justified.
- **Two examiners** appointed and a **28-day interim order** from 13 November 2026.
sections.Use it for:
- **crime.4.8** — NSW's high-risk terrorism offender scheme; supervision of people not convicted of terrorism.
- **Balance** — liberty and rehabilitation against community protection.
sections.Caution: A **class case summary of an interim order**; the allegations and any final order are undecided.

items.title: Staunton v El Matari [2026] FCA 1622 — an interim control order on release after terrorism offences
items.citation: [2026] FCA 1622 (Shariff J; order 29 October 2026, reasons 5 November 2026)
items.significance: Due for release after 7 years 4 months for terrorism offences, Isaac El Matari was placed under an interim control order — protective, not penal — with every condition tested for necessity and proportion.
items.document: Cases/Crime/Staunton v El Matari [2026] FCA 1622 - Case Summary.pdf
items.document11: Cases/Year 11/Year 11 - Staunton v El Matari [2026] FCA 1622 - Case Summary.pdf
items.lead:
In 2017, aged 18, **Isaac El Matari** travelled to Lebanon intending to join Islamic State; after returning he prepared
for terrorism and foreign incursion offences and was convicted in 2021. His sentence expired on **1 November 2026**. A
senior AFP member sought an **interim control order**; he did not oppose it.
items.use_it_for:
- **crime.4.8 (post-sentencing)** — Commonwealth control orders beside state supervision orders (see *Mustapha*, McKenna).
- **Rights** — liberty limited for what a person might do, decided on the balance of probabilities.
items.caution: A **class case summary of an interim order**; parts of the reasons are redacted and publication is restricted.

sections.Held — interim order made (29 October 20:
- He had a **terrorism-related conviction** (s 104.4(1)(c)(iv)).
- Every condition — where he lives, who he mixes with, **electronic monitoring** (ss 104.5A–104.5D) — and their combined
  effect was **reasonably necessary and reasonably appropriate and adapted** to protect the public.
- The scheme is **protective, not penal** (*Thomas v Mowbray*); past conduct is the best guide to risk. Confirmation hearing:
  **17 December 2026**.
sections.Use it for:
- **crime.4.8 (post-sentencing)** — Commonwealth control orders beside state supervision orders (see *Mustapha*, McKenna).
- **Rights** — liberty limited for what a person might do, decided on the balance of probabilities.
sections.Caution: A **class case summary of an interim order**; parts of the reasons are redacted and publication is restricted.

items.title: SafeWork NSW v Axentra Projects Pty Ltd [2026] NSWDC 398
items.significance: A formwork company was fined $75,000 (after a 25% plea discount) and ordered to publish a notice after a 16-year-old trainee fell 3.4 metres.
items.document: Cases/Crime/SafeWork NSW v Axentra Projects [2026] NSWDC 398 - Case Summary (updated 7Nov26).pdf
items.document11: Cases/Year 11/Year 11 - SafeWork NSW v Axentra Projects [2026] NSWDC 398 - Case Summary (updated 7Nov26).pdf
items.lead:
A formwork subcontractor pleaded guilty under s 32 of the *Work Health and Safety Act 2011* (NSW) after a
16-year-old trainee fell about 3.4 metres through a formwork deck on 19 May 2022. The maximum penalty
at the time was $1,782,579.
items.use_it_for:
- **crime.4.2 and 4.3** — deterrence and the factors for sentencing a corporation.
- **crime.4.6** — fines and adverse publicity orders as penalties.
- **Compliance** — how courts respond when a business fails a statutory safety duty.
items.caution:
The judgment cites s 21A(2)(g) and s 21A(2)(ib) for the same finding, and the notice size and cost text
is garbled. The amount of costs is not in the file. A child worker was injured; keep to the legal test.

sections.Held — Strathdee DCJ:
- The risk of falls through formwork decks was "well known, and as such, foreseeable"; the controls were
  relatively straightforward, and the failures were "manifold and systemic".
- The fine was set at **$100,000**, reduced by **25%** for the plea to **$75,000**. No deduction for
  capacity to pay.
- Half the fine goes to the prosecutor, the company pays costs, and a **public notice** (s 236) is
  published in the Sunday Sydney Morning Herald.
sections.Use it for:
- **crime.4.2 and 4.3** — deterrence and the factors for sentencing a corporation.
- **crime.4.6** — fines and adverse publicity orders as penalties.
- **Compliance** — how courts respond when a business fails a statutory safety duty.

The judgment cites s 21A(2)(g) and s 21A(2)(ib) for the same finding, and the notice size and cost text

items.title: Priestley v Blackfisch Films Pty Ltd [2026] NSWCATAD 343 — race discrimination claims fail on contractor status
items.citation: [2026] NSWCATAD 343 (M W Anderson, Senior Member, and M Maher, General Member; 6 November 2026)
items.significance: Two Gomeroi applicants claimed race discrimination against an Aboriginal-owned film company; the Tribunal found they were contractors, rejected the alleged slurs and dismissed the claims as lacking substance.
core_labels: The role of courts and tribunals
items.document: Cases/Human Rights/Priestley v Blackfisch Films Pty Ltd [2026] NSWCATAD 343 - Case Summary.pdf
items.document11: Cases/Year 11/Year 11 - Priestley v Blackfisch Films Pty Ltd [2026] NSWCATAD 343 - Case Summary.pdf
items.lead:
**Matthew Priestley** (a director from 2018) and **Mika Tyson** worked with **Blackfisch Films**, run by Ms Rutter, who also
has Gomeroi ancestry. After an argument over office cleanliness (September 2024) the locks were changed, after a plan to divert
a film project was found. The Fair Work Commission found no dismissal (January 2026). The applicants alleged race
discrimination in pay, remarks (including being called "too black") and exclusion.
items.use_it_for:
- **hr.2.11 / hr.2.9** — enforcing race discrimination law through NCAT, and the importance of proof and categories
  (employee v contractor).
items.caution: A **class case summary**; the slurs are alleged, not found.

sections.Held — claims dismissed (s 102):
- They were **contract workers** (s 10), not employees (s 8), which set the comparators.
- The alleged slurs were **not found**; the "too black" remark was about activism, not race; the lock-out followed the
  project-diversion plan.
- Estoppel from the Fair Work findings was not decided.
sections.Use it for:
- **hr.2.11 / hr.2.9** — enforcing race discrimination law through NCAT, and the importance of proof and categories
  (employee v contractor).
sections.Caution: A **class case summary**; the slurs are alleged, not found.

items.title: Australian Dance Arts Pty Ltd v Gincop Nominees 3 Pty Ltd [2026] NSWSC 1379 — boom-gate data fails to prove breach
items.citation: [2026] NSWSC 1379 (Pike J, Equity Division, Real Property List; 6 November 2026)
items.significance: A landlord ended a dance academy's car parking licence on boom-gate records; the court held the landlord had to prove breach on the balance of probabilities, and its unreliable data did not.
core_labels: The burden and standard of proof in civil law
Types of civil law — torts and contracts
items.document11: Cases/Year 11/Year 11 - Australian Dance Arts Pty Ltd v Gincop Nominees 3 Pty Ltd [2026] NSWSC 1379 - Case Summary.pdf
items.lead:
A dance academy in St Leonards leased premises in 2022 with a licence for **17 car spaces**. The new landlord terminated the
licence in September 2025, saying customers used more than the academy's seven rooftop spaces, relying on **boom-gate access
records** from the parking operator. The academy sought a declaration that the termination was void.
items.use_it_for:
- **Year 11 (Disputes under the law — civil)** — contracts, the burden and standard of proof, and remedies (declarations).
  Not an HSC topic.
items.caution: A **class case summary**; final orders were pending.

sections.Held — breach not proved:
- The **landlord bore the onus** of proving breach, even though the tenant brought the case.
- The ordinary **balance of probabilities** applied (*Evidence Act* s 140; *Briginshaw* did not raise it here).
- The access records — with known reader faults — were **unreliable** and not proof of where cars parked. The licence remains;
  the academy gets its costs.
sections.Use it for:
- **Year 11 (Disputes under the law — civil)** — contracts, the burden and standard of proof, and remedies (declarations).
  Not an HSC topic.
sections.Caution: A **class case summary**; final orders were pending.

items.title: Grayson Family Ltd Partnership LLLP v Lynch [2026] FCA 1667 — no standing to sue for the company
items.significance: Two shareholders sought leave to sue on behalf of a mining company over a 2020 share placement; they were not members, a late affidavit was refused as unfair, and the application was dismissed.
core_labels: The burden and standard of proof in civil law
Procedures in NSW tribunals and civil courts, including alternative dispute resolution
items.document11: Cases/Year 11/Year 11 - Grayson Family Ltd Partnership LLLP v Lynch [2026] FCA 1667 - Case Summary.pdf
items.lead:
In June 2020 **Citigold**, a mining company, placed 150 million shares at $0.005; the price later rose to $0.012. In 2026 a
family partnership and a trustee sought **leave under s 237** of the *Corporations Act* to sue directors and others **on behalf
of the company**.
items.use_it_for:
- **Year 11 (Disputes under the law — civil)** — standing, procedural fairness in evidence, and the burden of proof in civil
  proceedings. Not an HSC topic.
items.caution: A **class case summary**; insider trading was never proved and costs are still to be decided.

sections.Held — application dismissed:
- They were **not members**, or persons entitled to be registered, so had **no standing** (s 236(1)(a)).
- An affidavit prepared over lunch on the hearing day was **refused** as unfairly prejudicial to the respondents.
- In any case there was **no serious question to be tried** (s 237(2)(d)). Costs are reserved.
sections.Use it for:
- **Year 11 (Disputes under the law — civil)** — standing, procedural fairness in evidence, and the burden of proof in civil
  proceedings. Not an HSC topic.
sections.Caution: A **class case summary**; insider trading was never proved and costs are still to be decided.
